questions.question: What does ETL stand for in data engineering?
options: Extract, Transfer, Load
Export, Transform, Log
Extract, Transform, Load
Extract, Test, Launch
questions.explanation: ETL means Extract data from sources, Transform it (clean, join, aggregate) and Load it into a target such as a warehouse; 'Transfer' is a common mix-up, but the T is the transformation step.

questions.question: What is a data warehouse primarily designed for?
options: Archiving database backups that are rarely read, for disaster recovery
Analytical querying and reporting across integrated historical data
Streaming events from producers to consumers in real time
Caching session data so that web pages load faster
questions.explanation: A warehouse integrates cleaned, historical data from many sources and is optimized for analytical (OLAP) queries and reporting; backups are kept for recovery rather than for querying, and real-time event delivery is the job of a broker such as Kafka.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a primary key in a relational table?
options: Reference a matching row in another table
Keep rows physically stored in insertion order
Allow NULL values to mark incomplete rows
Uniquely identify each row in the table
questions.explanation: A primary key is a unique, non-NULL column (or set of columns) that identifies each row; referencing a row in another table is what a foreign key does.

questions.question: What best describes stream processing?
options: Processing a full day's accumulated files in one scheduled nightly run
Processing data continuously, in near real time, as events arrive
Copying a database to a standby server for failover
Running ad-hoc SQL queries over historical warehouse data
questions.explanation: Stream processing handles each event (or small micro-batch) shortly after it arrives, e.g. Kafka with Flink or Spark Structured Streaming; collecting a day's data and processing it on a schedule is batch processing.

questions.question: JSON is commonly described as what type of data format?
options: Semi-structured
Structured, with a fixed tabular schema
Unstructured
Columnar binary
questions.explanation: JSON records carry their own keys and may nest objects or arrays and vary in fields, so JSON is semi-structured rather than a fixed-schema table; 'columnar binary' describes formats such as Parquet.

questions.question: In a star schema, what typically distinguishes a fact table from dimension tables?
options: Fact tables hold descriptive text attributes, while dimensions hold numeric measures
Fact tables are normalized to 3NF, while dimension tables are never joined
The fact table records measurable events with foreign keys to descriptive dimensions
Dimension tables record each business event, while the fact table stores lookup codes
questions.explanation: A fact table stores measurements of business events (e.g. quantity, amount) at a defined grain plus foreign keys to dimensions such as date, customer and product, which hold the descriptive attributes; the first option has the roles reversed.

questions.question: How can partitioning a large table by date improve many analytical queries?
options: Queries filtered on date scan only the matching partitions (partition pruning)
It compresses every column so that no index is ever needed
It sorts all rows so that joins on any column avoid shuffles
It keeps recent partitions cached in memory so that every query runs in constant time
questions.explanation: With date partitions, a filter such as WHERE event_date = '2026-09-30' lets the engine skip every other partition and read far less data; partitioning does not make queries constant-time or remove the need for good filters.

questions.question: Why is a columnar format such as Parquet often efficient for analytics?
options: Each row is stored contiguously, so whole records are fetched in one read
Files are plain text, so any tool can parse them without a schema
Every write updates rows in place, avoiding rewrites of whole files
Queries read only needed columns, and similar values compress well
questions.explanation: Parquet stores each column's values together, so a query touching 3 of 50 columns reads only those columns, and same-typed values compress well; storing whole rows contiguously is the row-oriented layout of CSV files and OLTP tables.

questions.question: A Kafka consumer calls commitSync() as soon as poll() returns a batch, and only then processes the records. It crashes halfway through a batch, and the group restarts it. What happens to the records it had not processed yet?
options: They are re-delivered, because Kafka tracks an acknowledgement for each record
They are read again from the start of the topic when the consumer restarts
They are deleted from the partition, because their offsets were committed
They are skipped, because the group resumes after the committed offset
questions.explanation: The committed offset is where the group resumes, so committing before processing means a crash skips the unprocessed records (at-most-once); committing after processing gives at-least-once instead. Kafka tracks one offset per partition rather than per-record acks, and reading a record never deletes it.

questions.question: In Apache Airflow, what does a DAG represent?
options: A workflow of tasks and the dependencies between them
A single operator that runs one SQL statement
A stored connection to an external system such as a database
A queue of messages waiting to be consumed by workers
questions.explanation: A DAG (directed acyclic graph) defines a pipeline: its tasks plus the dependency edges and schedule that decide the run order, with no cycles allowed; operators are the individual tasks and connections store credentials.

questions.question: What is Change Data Capture (CDC) used for?
options: Taking a full snapshot of the database every night for backups
Detecting schema changes in source tables and automatically blocking the whole pipeline
Capturing each row-level change in a source so downstream copies stay in sync
Auditing which users edited a dashboard's configuration
questions.explanation: CDC captures row-level changes (inserts, updates and deletes), often by reading the database's transaction log (e.g. with Debezium), so warehouses, caches or search indexes can apply just the changes instead of reloading full snapshots.

questions.question: What does it mean for a data pipeline operation to be idempotent?
options: It can run only once, so the scheduler must never retry it
Re-running it with the same input gives the same end state, with no duplicates
It always appends its output, so the results of every run are preserved
It processes every row in its own separate transaction so partial loads never happen
questions.explanation: An idempotent step (e.g. overwriting a date partition or a MERGE on a key) can be retried or backfilled safely because a second run with the same input produces the same final state; blind appends create duplicates on every retry.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Type 2 Slowly Changing Dimension?
options: Preserve history by adding a new row version when tracked attributes change
Overwrite the old attribute value in place, so only the latest value is kept
Store the current and the previous value side by side in two separate columns
Move changed rows into a separate archive table and delete them from the dimension
questions.explanation: SCD Type 2 inserts a new row (new surrogate key, effective dates or a current flag) each time a tracked attribute changes, so facts keep pointing at the version valid at the time; overwriting is Type 1 and a 'previous value' column is Type 3.

questions.question: Why can a shuffle be expensive in Apache Spark?
options: It collects all of the rows onto the driver, which then processes them on a single machine
It re-reads the original input files from storage for every downstream stage
It moves data between executors over the network, with serialization and disk writes
It turns off Catalyst optimization for the remaining stages of the job
questions.explanation: Wide transformations such as groupBy, join or repartition write partitioned shuffle files to disk, and the next stage fetches them over the network, adding serialization, I/O and a stage boundary; the data is not pulled onto the driver.

questions.question: What is a watermark commonly used for in event-time stream processing?
options: Reordering all events by processing time instead of by event time
Committing the consumer's offsets back to Kafka after each micro-batch
Tagging each event with a checksum so consumers can detect tampering
Deciding how long to wait for late events before a window is finalized
questions.explanation: A watermark (e.g. latest event time seen minus 10 minutes) sets how much lateness to tolerate: once it passes a window's end, the window is finalized and its state dropped, and later events are treated as too late.

questions.question: After `GROUP BY customer_id`, which clause keeps only the customers with more than 5 orders?
options: WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
GROUP BY COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY COUNT(*) > 5
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test COUNT(*); WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot contain aggregate functions, and ORDER BY only sorts.

questions.question:
What does this Python code print?

emails = ['a@x.com', 'b@x.com', 'a@x.com', 'c@x.com']
print(len(set(emails)))
options: It raises a TypeError
questions.explanation: A set keeps only unique values, so the duplicate 'a@x.com' is stored once and len() returns 3; strings are hashable, so no TypeError is raised.

questions.question: A transfer debits account A and then credits account B inside one database transaction. The server crashes after the debit but before the commit. Which ACID property guarantees that the debit is undone?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
questions.explanation: Atomicity makes a transaction all-or-nothing, so an uncommitted transaction is rolled back during recovery and the half-done debit disappears; durability only protects changes that were already committed.

questions.question: The table events(user_id, event_time, payload) contains repeated rows. Which approach keeps only the latest row for each user_id?
options: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM events ORDER BY event_time DESC
GROUP BY user_id, payload and keep MAX(event_time) for each group
Filter RANK() OVER (ORDER BY event_time DESC) = 1 computed over the whole table
Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time DESC) = 1
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by user_id and ordered by event_time DESC numbers each user's rows from the newest, so keeping 1 leaves exactly one latest row per user; a RANK over the whole table finds only the globally latest rows, and DISTINCT removes only fully identical rows.

questions.question: In PostgreSQL, `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42` is slow on a 50-million-row table, and EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What is the most direct fix?
options: Add ORDER BY customer_id to the query
Create a B-tree index on orders(customer_id)
Change SELECT * to SELECT DISTINCT *
Run the query inside an explicit transaction
questions.explanation: Without an index on customer_id the planner must read every row; a B-tree index lets it jump straight to the few matching rows with an index scan. Sorting, DISTINCT or a transaction do not reduce the rows scanned.

questions.question: A Python script must process a 50 GB log file on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Call f.read() once and split the text on newlines
Loop with `for line in f:` and process one line at a time
Load all lines with f.readlines() and loop over the list
Read the file into a pandas DataFrame with one pd.read_csv() call
questions.explanation: A file object is a lazy iterator, so `for line in f:` keeps only a small buffer in memory at a time; read(), readlines() and a single read_csv() call all try to load the whole 50 GB into 8 GB of RAM (pandas would need chunksize= to stream).

questions.question: In PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED isolation level, transaction T1 runs the same SELECT twice. Between the two, transaction T2 updates one of those rows and commits. What can T1 observe?
options: Both SELECTs return identical rows, because T1 uses one snapshot for the whole transaction
T2's UPDATE waits until T1 commits, because T1 has read the row
The second SELECT sees T2's committed change (a non-repeatable read)
T1 could have seen T2's change even before T2 committed (a dirty read)
questions.explanation: Under READ COMMITTED each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so the second SELECT sees data committed in between (a non-repeatable read); one snapshot per transaction is REPEATABLE READ behaviour, plain SELECTs do not block writers, and PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads.

`id NOT IN (2, NULL)` means id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, and any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, so no row passes the filter. NOT EXISTS (or excluding NULLs in the subquery) returns the expected ids 1 and 3.

questions.question: A PostgreSQL table has one B-tree index on (country, city). Which WHERE clause benefits least from this index?
options: WHERE country = 'IN' AND city = 'Pune'
WHERE city = 'Pune'
WHERE country = 'IN'
WHERE country = 'IN' AND city LIKE 'Pu%'
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree is sorted by country first and by city within each country, so it can seek on any leftmost prefix; a filter on city alone cannot seek directly and at best skip-scans every country (PostgreSQL 18+) or falls back to a sequential scan.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

add_tag('raw')
print(add_tag('clean'))
options: ['clean']
['clean', 'raw']
It raises a TypeError
['raw', 'clean']
questions.explanation: A default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so both calls append to the same list and the second call returns ['raw', 'clean']; use tags=None and create a new list inside the function instead.

questions.question: Which workload is typical of an OLTP system rather than an OLAP system?
options: A monthly revenue report that scans two years of sales
A dashboard that aggregates KPIs by region and quarter
Many small order inserts and updates per second from a checkout app
Ad-hoc analysis of customer churn trends across five years of history
questions.explanation: OLTP systems (e.g. PostgreSQL behind an app) handle many short read/write transactions on individual rows; large scans and aggregations over history for reports and dashboards are OLAP workloads that belong in a warehouse.

questions.question: What is the main goal of normalizing a relational schema to third normal form (3NF)?
options: Reduce redundancy and update anomalies by storing each fact in one place
Speed up analytical queries by pre-joining all tables into one wide table
Store every table in a compressed columnar format
Keep the full history of every row by versioning each change
questions.explanation: Normalization splits data into related tables so each fact (e.g. a customer's address) is stored once, avoiding insert, update and delete anomalies; pre-joining into wide tables is denormalization, which warehouses use to speed up reads.

questions.question: How does a snowflake schema differ from a star schema?
options: It has several fact tables but no dimension tables
It stores every dimension as a JSON column inside the fact table
It can be queried only in the Snowflake data warehouse
Its dimension tables are normalized into further related tables
questions.explanation: In a snowflake schema a dimension is split into sub-tables (e.g. product, category, department), which saves space but adds joins; in a star schema each dimension is one denormalized table. The name has nothing to do with the Snowflake product.

questions.question: While documenting a fact_sales table for analysts, you must state its grain. Which statement is a correct grain declaration?
options: The table holds all of the company's sales data from 2020 onwards
Each row is loaded within 15 minutes of the order being placed
Each row represents one order line item (one product on one order)
The table joins to the date, customer and product dimensions
questions.explanation: The grain states exactly what one fact row represents and must be declared before choosing dimensions and measures; scope, load latency and related dimensions are useful documentation but do not define the grain.

questions.question: fact_account_balance is a daily snapshot that stores every account's closing balance for each day, together with the account's branch. Which logic gives each branch's total balance at the end of September?
options: Sum balance across the branch's accounts using only the 30 September rows
Sum balance across all of the branch's rows for every day in September
Take MAX(balance) across all of the branch's rows in September
Average each account's balance over September, then sum those averages
questions.explanation: A balance is semi-additive: it can be summed across accounts and branches but not across time, so use the snapshot for the last day of the period; summing every day counts each balance about 30 times, and MAX or average balances answer different questions.

questions.question: fact_orders stores customer_id (the natural key) and order_date. dim_customer keeps every version of each customer, with valid_from, valid_to and is_current columns (the current row has valid_to = '9999-12-31'). To report revenue by the city each customer lived in when the order was placed, how should the two tables be joined?
options: Match customer_id and keep only rows where d.is_current = true
Match customer_id and require valid_from <= order_date < valid_to
Match customer_id and keep the version with the earliest valid_from
Match customer_id only, since each customer appears in the dimension once
questions.explanation: In this SCD Type 2 dimension each order must match the customer version whose validity range contains the order date; is_current restates all history with today's city, and joining on customer_id alone multiplies each order by every version of that customer.

questions.question: fact_orders stores each order once with its order_amount, while fact_shipments stores every shipment, and one order can ship in several parts. An analyst joins them on order_id and runs SUM(order_amount). What goes wrong?
options: Each order's amount is counted once per shipment, inflating revenue
The join silently drops every order that was shipped in several parts
SUM ignores order_amount whenever the shipment columns are NULL
Nothing, because order_id is the primary key of fact_orders
questions.explanation: Joining order-level data to shipment-level data repeats each order once per shipment (fan-out), so the sum double-counts; aggregate both facts to a common grain before joining. A key that is unique on one side does not prevent duplication from the other side.

questions.question: In BigQuery with on-demand (bytes-scanned) pricing, which change reduces the bytes billed for `SELECT * FROM sales WHERE region = 'South' LIMIT 10` on an unpartitioned, unclustered table?
options: Changing LIMIT 10 to LIMIT 1
Adding ORDER BY region
Adding a second filter such as AND year = 2025 to the WHERE clause
Selecting only the three columns needed instead of *
questions.explanation: BigQuery is columnar and bills for every byte in the columns a query reads; on an unpartitioned, unclustered table, LIMIT, ORDER BY and extra filters do not reduce the data scanned, but reading fewer columns does.

questions.question: What is the key difference between ELT and ETL?
options: In ELT, data is transformed on a separate server before it is ever loaded
ELT skips the transform step and only copies data between systems
In ELT, raw data is loaded first and transformed inside the warehouse
ELT works only for streaming data, while ETL works only for batch
questions.explanation: ELT lands raw data in the warehouse or lakehouse and runs transformations there (often as SQL models in dbt) using its scalable compute; transforming on a separate engine before loading is classic ETL.

questions.question: Which pair of built-in dbt data tests checks that order_id can serve as a model's primary key?
options: unique and not_null
accepted_values and relationships
not_null and accepted_values
relationships and unique
questions.explanation: A primary key must be present and distinct in every row, which is exactly what not_null and unique assert; accepted_values checks values against an allowed list, and relationships checks foreign keys against another model.

questions.question: In a dbt model, what does `{{ ref('stg_orders') }}` do?
options: Copies every row of stg_orders into the current model's table at compile time
Resolves to the stg_orders relation and records it as an upstream dependency
Runs the data tests defined on stg_orders before this model is built
Imports a Python function named stg_orders into the SQL file
questions.explanation: ref() compiles to the fully qualified name of stg_orders in the target environment and tells dbt this model depends on it, so models build in the right order and lineage is tracked; it does not copy data or run tests.

questions.question: A nightly job copies a source orders table that has a reliable updated_at column. Which approach loads only new and changed rows?
options: Truncate the target table and reload the full source table every night
Extract only the rows whose created_at falls on today's date
Extract the 10,000 rows with the highest order_id each night
Extract rows with updated_at above the last run's high-water mark
questions.explanation: Saving the maximum updated_at loaded so far (a high-water mark, often with a small overlap) and extracting only newer rows picks up both inserts and updates; filtering on created_at misses updates, and a full reload works but is not incremental.

questions.question: A daily Airflow DAG has a start_date 30 days in the past and catchup=True. What happens when it is first unpaused?
options: Only today's run is scheduled, and all of the past intervals are skipped
A single DAG run is created that processes all 30 of the missed days in one go
The scheduler creates runs for each missed daily interval since start_date
The DAG fails to load because its start_date lies in the past
questions.explanation: With catchup=True the scheduler creates a run for every data interval between start_date and now that has no run yet (limited by max_active_runs); with catchup=False only the most recent interval is scheduled, and recent Airflow versions default to False, which is why it is set explicitly here.

questions.question: A daily task runs `INSERT INTO sales SELECT * FROM staging_sales WHERE sale_date = '{{ ds }}'`. After the run is retried, that day's totals are doubled. Which change makes the task idempotent?
options: Set retries=0 so that Airflow can never run the task a second time
Add DISTINCT to the SELECT so each staging row is inserted only once
Delete that date's rows and re-insert them within one transaction
Wrap the INSERT alone in a transaction so a failed run never commits
questions.explanation: Replacing the whole sale_date slice (DELETE + INSERT in one transaction, a partition overwrite, or a MERGE on a key) gives the same result however many times it runs; DISTINCT only removes duplicates within one run, and a transaction around the INSERT alone does not stop a successful re-run from appending again.

questions.question: Why is log-based CDC (e.g. Debezium reading the PostgreSQL write-ahead log) often preferred over query-based CDC that repeatedly polls the source tables for recently changed rows?
options: It works without any access to the source database or its transaction logs
It captures hard deletes and every update without repeated table scans
It lets source tables skip primary keys, since changes are captured by position
It removes the need to handle schema changes in downstream consumers
questions.explanation: Reading the transaction log streams every insert, update and delete in commit order with little load on the source; polling on a timestamp column misses hard deletes and intermediate updates between polls, and depends on every writer setting that column correctly.

questions.question: A dbt incremental model selects source rows whose updated_at is newer than the max in {{ this }}, but no unique_key is configured. An order that was updated in the source is picked up on the next run. What happens?
options: The updated order is appended, so the model now has two rows for it
dbt detects the existing order and updates it in place
The run fails because incremental models require a unique_key
The update is skipped because that order already exists in the model
questions.explanation: Without a unique_key, dbt's incremental run simply inserts the selected rows, so the new version sits next to the old one; setting unique_key='order_id' makes dbt merge (or delete+insert) on that key and replace the existing row.

questions.question: Why should an Airflow task select source data using the run's data interval (e.g. `{{ data_interval_start }}` or `{{ ds }}`) instead of calling datetime.now() inside the task?
options: Jinja templates make the task run faster than Python's datetime functions
Airflow forbids importing the datetime module anywhere inside a DAG file
Using now() makes the scheduler create overlapping runs of the same DAG
Retries and backfills of an old run then process that run's own dates
questions.explanation: Each DAG run has a fixed data interval, so retrying yesterday's run or backfilling last month reads exactly the same slice of data and produces the same result; datetime.now() changes on every execution, which breaks idempotency.

questions.question: In PySpark, which DataFrame call is an action that actually triggers a job to run?
options: df.filter(df.amount > 0)
df.select('order_id')
df.withColumn('year', year(df.ts))
df.count()
questions.explanation: filter, select and withColumn are lazy transformations that only build a logical plan; actions such as count(), collect(), show() or a write make Spark optimize the plan and run the job.

questions.question: In Apache Kafka, what is a topic?
options: A queue that deletes each message as soon as one consumer reads it
A named, append-only log of events, split into partitions
A group of consumers that share the work of reading data
A table of indexed rows that consumers update in place
questions.explanation: A topic is a named stream of records stored as partitioned, append-only logs; messages stay for the retention period whether or not they are read, and each consumer group tracks its own offsets, unlike a queue that deletes on read.

questions.question: A dashboard must show 'orders in the last 10 minutes', refreshed every minute. Which window type fits?
options: A 10-minute tumbling window with no overlap
A session window with a 10-minute inactivity gap
A 10-minute sliding window with a 1-minute slide
A single global window that is never closed
questions.explanation: A 10-minute sliding (hopping) window that advances every minute produces overlapping windows, giving a fresh last-10-minutes count each minute; a tumbling window updates only once per 10 minutes, and session windows group bursts of activity.

questions.question: All events for the same order_id must be consumed in the order they were produced. How should the producer publish them to a multi-partition topic?
options: Use order_id as the message key
Use a random key so events spread evenly across partitions
Raise the topic's replication factor to 3
Add more consumers to the consumer group
questions.explanation: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, and the default partitioner sends all records with the same key to the same partition, so keying by order_id keeps each order's events in sequence; random keys scatter them, and replication does not affect ordering.

questions.question: A PySpark DataFrame has 2,000 small partitions. Before writing, you want 20 output files without triggering a full shuffle. Which call fits?
options: df.repartition(20)
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', 20)
df.coalesce(20)
df.persist()
questions.explanation: coalesce(n) merges existing partitions into fewer ones without a shuffle, whereas repartition(n) always performs a full shuffle; spark.sql.shuffle.partitions only affects stages that shuffle, and persist() just caches the data.

questions.question: A Kafka topic has 6 partitions, and a standard consumer group reading it has 8 consumers. What happens?
options: Each consumer reads 0.75 of a partition's messages
Six consumers get one partition each, and two stay idle
Kafka automatically adds two more partitions to the topic to match
All eight consumers read every message from all six partitions
questions.explanation: In a consumer group each partition is assigned to at most one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the partition count: six consumers work and two sit idle as standbys. To scale further you add partitions.

questions.question: A Spark job joins a 500 GB transactions DataFrame with a 20 MB countries lookup DataFrame, and the Spark UI shows a huge shuffle for the join. What is the usual fix?
options: Broadcast the small DataFrame with broadcast(countries)
Call repartition(1) on both DataFrames before the join
collect() the transactions to the driver and join in Python
Convert both DataFrames to pandas with toPandas()
questions.explanation: A broadcast hash join ships the small table to every executor so the large table is joined where it sits, without shuffling 500 GB (20 MB is above the default 10 MB auto-broadcast threshold, so the hint is needed); repartition(1), collect() or toPandas() funnel the data through a single task or machine.

questions.question: In a Spark join stage, 199 tasks finish in about a minute, but one task runs for 40 minutes. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Too few executors, so double the number of executors given to the job
The driver is short on memory, so raise spark.driver.memory
Parquet is slow to write, so write the output as CSV instead
Skew on the join key, so salt the hot key or enable AQE skew joins
questions.explanation: One straggler task means one partition holds far more rows, typically a hot join key such as NULL or one huge customer; salting that key or letting Adaptive Query Execution split skewed partitions spreads the work, whereas more executors cannot speed up a single task.

questions.question: A pipeline reads from Kafka, aggregates in a stream processor and writes to a database. Which design gives effectively exactly-once results even when tasks fail and replay data?
options: Producer acks=0, so messages are never sent twice
Consumer auto-commit with a very short commit interval
Checkpointed offsets plus an idempotent or transactional sink
At-least-once delivery with extra retries on every database write
questions.explanation: Failures cause replays, so exactly-once results come from tracking offsets together with state (checkpoints) and making the output idempotent (upsert by key) or transactional; acks=0 can lose data, and auto-commit or retries alone give at-most-once or at-least-once behaviour.

questions.question: What is a data lake?
options: A warehouse that only accepts cleaned and fully modeled relational tables
Cheap storage, usually cloud object storage, for raw data in any format
An in-memory cache placed in front of BI dashboards to speed them up
A message broker that delivers real-time events to many consumers
questions.explanation: A data lake keeps structured, semi-structured and unstructured data (CSV, JSON, Parquet, images, logs) in raw form on cheap storage such as Amazon S3 or ADLS, applying a schema when the data is read; a warehouse stores modeled tables.

questions.question: In a medallion (bronze/silver/gold) lakehouse architecture, what does the bronze layer usually hold?
options: Business-level aggregates that feed dashboards
Cleaned, deduplicated and conformed tables
Raw data ingested as-is from source systems
Trained machine learning model files
questions.explanation: Bronze stores raw source data as ingested (often append-only, with load metadata) so it can be reprocessed; silver holds cleaned and conformed data, and gold holds business-level aggregates and marts.

questions.question: Why do data teams package pipeline code as Docker images?
options: Code runs much faster inside a container than it does directly on the host
Code and dependencies run the same on a laptop, in CI and in production
The image stores the pipeline's output data permanently between runs
A container replaces the need for an orchestrator such as Airflow
questions.explanation: An image bundles the code with pinned library versions and the runtime, removing 'works on my machine' differences between development, CI and production; containers do not make code faster, should not hold output data, and still need an orchestrator to schedule them.

questions.question: Where should a production pipeline's database password be stored?
options: Hard-coded in the DAG file, since the Git repository is private
Baked into the Docker image as an ENV value at build time
In a config.yaml committed next to the pipeline code
In a secrets manager that the pipeline reads at runtime
questions.explanation: A secrets manager (e.g. AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault or an Airflow secrets backend) keeps credentials encrypted, access-controlled, audited and rotatable; anything committed to Git or baked into an image is exposed to everyone who can read the repo or pull the image.

questions.question: What do open table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg add on top of plain Parquet files in object storage?
options: ACID commits, schema evolution and time travel via a metadata layer
Conversion of the Parquet files into row-based CSV so they are readable
A dedicated database server that replaces the object storage underneath
Built-in BI dashboards generated automatically from every table
questions.explanation: Delta and Iceberg keep a transaction log or metadata tree recording which data files make up each table version, enabling atomic commits, MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE, schema evolution and time travel; the data itself stays as Parquet files in object storage.

questions.question: A streaming job writes thousands of 50 KB Parquet files per hour into a Delta table on S3, and queries keep getting slower. What is the usual fix?
options: Store the data as CSV instead, since engines open CSV files faster
Add minute and second partition columns to spread the files out
Periodically compact them into larger files, e.g. with OPTIMIZE
Move the bucket to a colder storage class to cut access costs
questions.explanation: Every tiny file adds open, list and metadata overhead, so engines spend more time handling files than reading data; compaction (Delta OPTIMIZE, Iceberg rewrite_data_files) rewrites them into files of roughly 128 MB to 1 GB, while finer partitions would create even more small files.

questions.question: In a CI/CD setup for a dbt project, what should run automatically on every pull request before it is merged?
options: A direct deployment to production that is rolled back if dashboards break
Nothing, because data tests should run only after merging, in production
A manual check of sample rows exported to a spreadsheet
dbt build for the changed models and their tests in an isolated CI schema
questions.explanation: CI should build and test the modified models (e.g. dbt build --select state:modified+) in a throwaway schema, so broken SQL or failing tests block the merge; testing only in production lets bad data reach users first.

questions.question: Before renaming a column in a silver table, an engineer checks the data lineage graph. What question does lineage answer here?
options: How long each query that reads the table takes to run on average
Which downstream models and dashboards depend on that column
Which users and roles currently have read access to the table
How much the table costs to store in object storage each month
questions.explanation: Lineage maps how data flows from sources through transformations to reports, at table or column level, so you can see the impact of a change before making it; latency, access grants and storage cost come from monitoring, IAM and billing tools.

questions.question: Every Airflow task in a daily pipeline succeeded, but the upstream export file was empty, so the dashboard silently showed stale numbers. Which check would have caught this?
options: A row-count check that alerts when a load is far below normal
An alert when warehouse CPU utilisation goes above 90 percent
A CI step that checks every DAG file parses without import errors
Unit tests for the Python helper functions used by the tasks
questions.explanation: Task success only proves the code ran; data checks on volume and freshness (row count far below usual, or max(loaded_at) older than expected) catch empty or late inputs, while CPU alerts, DAG parsing and unit tests would all pass here.

questions.question: A 20 TB clickstream dataset is stored as Parquet on Amazon S3 and queried with Athena. Nearly every query filters on a date range, and user_id has 10 million distinct values. Which partitioning scheme is the best choice?
options: Partition by user_id, so that each user's events sit in their own folder
Partition by event timestamp down to the second, for the finest pruning
Partition by event_date, the column that almost every query filters on
Leave it unpartitioned, since Parquet min/max statistics make partitions redundant
questions.explanation: Partition on a low-to-moderate-cardinality column that queries filter on, so Athena reads only the matching dates from reasonably large files; user_id or per-second partitions create millions of tiny files whose listing and planning overhead swamps the reads, and without partitions every query must still list and open every file.

questions.question: A bad job overwrote a Delta Lake table 10 days ago and nobody noticed. VACUUM runs every night with the default 7-day retention. What happens if you now RESTORE the table to the version before the bad write?
options: It fails, because VACUUM has already deleted the data files that version needs
It succeeds, because the transaction log stores a full copy of each version's rows
It succeeds, because VACUUM only removes files that no table version ever referenced
It fails, because Delta Lake keeps no table history older than 24 hours
questions.explanation: VACUUM permanently deletes data files that the current version no longer references once they are older than the retention period (7 days by default), so the pre-overwrite files are gone and RESTORE to that version fails. The log stores only metadata, so its 30-day history cannot bring the files back.

questions.question: Raw files on Amazon S3 are read often during their first 30 days, almost never afterwards, and must be kept for 7 years for compliance. Which setup meets this at the lowest cost?
options: Keep every object in S3 Standard so that all files stay instantly readable
Upload every file straight to Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest storage class
Delete files after 30 days and re-ingest them from the source when needed
A lifecycle rule: Standard-IA after 30 days, Glacier later, delete after 7 years
questions.explanation: Lifecycle rules move objects to cheaper classes as access drops and expire them when retention ends, so you pay Standard prices only while files are hot; Deep Archive from day one makes the frequent early reads slow (restores take hours) and costly, and deleting early breaks the 7-year retention.

questions.question: Analysts must query a customers table but must not see raw phone numbers, while a small fraud team needs the real values. What is the best approach in a warehouse such as Snowflake or BigQuery?
options: Rely on encryption at rest, which hides the raw phone numbers from analysts
A role-based masking policy on the column, unmasked for the fraud role
Drop the phone column for everyone, including the fraud team
Ask analysts not to select the column and review query logs monthly
questions.explanation: Dynamic data masking (Snowflake masking policies, BigQuery column-level data masking) enforces least privilege on one governed table: other roles see masked values and the fraud role sees real ones. Encryption at rest is transparent to anyone allowed to query the table, and a request nobody enforces is not a control.
